Supreme Court Blocks Trump-Backed Missouri Map Again

2026-W37 12 outlets SRQ
0.90 V2×20 V3×2 V5×1

The U.S. Supreme Court again rejected Missouri's Republican-drawn congressional map, requiring the state to use census-era districts for the November election.

Full Narration

The U.S. Supreme Court rejected Missouri's Trump-backed congressional map for the second time, blocking its use in November's elections. The Missouri Supreme Court had already ruled in September that the state must revert to districts drawn after the last census. What this means for Missouri voters: the November election will proceed under the census-era map, not the Republican-redrawn version. The U.S. Supreme Court's refusal to intervene on appeal leaves that outcome intact. The test now is whether Missouri Republicans pursue any further legal avenue before the November deadline, or whether the census-era map stands through the full election cycle. The Court's position, stated twice, is on record.

Full Narration

The CDC declared this week that the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak on record is over. 12,883 people were sickened across 21 states since May 1st. 2 people died in Michigan. The outbreak was tied to shredded iceberg lettuce grown by Taylor Farms in Mexico. That linkage is corroborated by multiple outlets and verified independently. The scale, 12,883 cases, makes this the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak the CDC has recorded. The declaration that it's over is the CDC's official position. For anyone who experienced unexplained gastrointestinal illness this summer across those 21 states, that sourcing trail now points to a specific product and a specific grower.

Court Strikes Down Trump Order on Michigan Coal Plant

2026-W37 8 outlets SRQ
0.59 V1×14 V2×4

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit struck down a Trump administration emergency order that had kept a Michigan coal-fired power plant open past its scheduled retirement.

Full Narration

A federal appeals court struck down the Trump administration's emergency order keeping a Michigan coal plant open past its scheduled retirement date. The ruling came from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, and it's verified by independent fact-checkers. The court found the Energy Department exceeded its authority in forcing the plant to remain operational. The plant had been scheduled for retirement before the administration invoked emergency powers to override that timeline. The administration's options now include appealing to the Supreme Court or seeking a different statutory mechanism. The D.C. Circuit's finding on authority is on record. Whether the administration pursues a second legal route is the next decision point to watch.
